readings.title: The Greedy Shepherd — Part 1: Clutch and Kind
readings.challenge: Listen for what each brother’s name tells you about him.
readings.focus: Two shepherd brothers, one grasping and one gentle, and a flock that begins to disappear.
readings.context: From Frances Browne’s Granny’s Wonderful Chair (1857), a book of fairy tales. A girl named Snowflower has a magic chair that tells stories when she asks it, and this is one of them. Because the chair is speaking, every paragraph begins with a quotation mark, and the people in the story speak inside single quotation marks. A shepherd looks after sheep with a crook, a hooked stick, and a pipe, a simple flute. Sheep are sheared, or clipped, with shears like big scissors, to take their wool, which grows back. A ewe is a mother sheep. Covetous means always wanting more for yourself. A dispute is an argument, and the folding is when sheep are shut in their pen at night.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Greedy Shepherd,” from the start to the sheep beginning to stray; opens “"Once upon a time there lived in the south country two brothers, whose business it was to…”; closes “…to go; and, count the flock when they might, some were sure to be missed at the folding.”.

questions.prompt: What are the two brothers called? How do the names fit them?
facilitatorNotes: Clutch, who grabs and holds on to everything for himself, and Kind, who would share his last bite with a hungry dog.
evidence: one of whom was called Clutch, and the other Kind
Kind would have shared his last morsel with a hungry dog

questions.prompt: What happens after the traders praise Clutch’s wool and pay the highest price?
facilitatorNotes: He clips the sheep closer and more often, leaving them bare even when the days turn cold.
evidence: he left the poor sheep as bare as if they had been shaven

questions.prompt: Why does Kind not quarrel with Clutch over their father’s sheep?
facilitatorNotes: He would rather keep the peace than fight for sheep, so he works as a helper. Some children will think he should stand up for himself; he does argue later, for the sheep.
evidence: Kind wouldn't quarrel with his brother for the sake of the sheep

questions.prompt: Which sheep are the first to go missing? What might that mean?
facilitatorNotes: The closest clipped. Perhaps the cold, bare sheep are leaving, or something is taking them away from a greedy master. The story has not said yet; let children guess.
evidence: the closest clipped were the first to go

readings.title: The Greedy Shepherd — Part 2: Up the hills
readings.challenge: Watch where Kind looks when he is sad, and what he sees there.
readings.focus: With nothing left, the brothers climb the hills no shepherd has crossed, and music leads them to a wonder.
readings.context: Recap: Clutch, the greedy elder brother, clipped his sheep so close and so often that they shivered bare, while kind-hearted Kind tried to stop him. Then their sheep began to stray away and vanish, the closest-clipped first. The story is still being told by Snowflower’s magic chair. Vexation is annoyance. A cleft is a deep crack in a hillside, and to scour up it is to run up it fast. A moorland or heath is wild open land; a pasture is a grassy field. A countenance is a face.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Greedy Shepherd,” from the flock melting away to the brothers finding the ancient shepherd; opens “"Kind grew tired of watching, and Clutch lost his sleep with vexation. The other…”; closes “…he had the countenance of one who had led a quiet life, and known no cares nor losses.”.

questions.prompt: How many sheep are left by spring? What does Clutch want to do with them?
facilitatorNotes: Three old, lame ewes; he wants to shear even them, though it is still cold.
evidence: Brother, there is wool to be had on their backs.

questions.prompt: Where does Kind look for comfort, and what does he see there?
facilitatorNotes: Up at the great hills at sunset, and he sees three sheep-like creatures run up a cleft as fast as deer.
evidence: three creatures like sheep scoured up a cleft in one of them as fleet as any deer

questions.prompt: Why does Clutch decide to leave the plain? Why does Kind go too?
facilitatorNotes: Clutch will not stay to be looked down on for being poor. Kind would rather farm, but goes to keep his brother company.
evidence: I'll not stay on this plain to be despised for poverty.
he resolved to bear him company

questions.prompt: What happens to the brothers when they hear the music? What do they find at the top?
facilitatorNotes: Their sore feet and heavy hearts are healed, and they follow it to a violet pasture of white sheep and an old shepherd with snow-white hair and beard. Ask what makes it feel magical.
evidence: the soreness passed from their feet, and the heaviness from their hearts

readings.title: The Greedy Shepherd — Part 3: Shearing the wolves
readings.challenge: Listen to each brother answer the old shepherd, and who is brave when it matters.
readings.focus: A strange test shows which brother is the true shepherd, and the lost flock comes home.
readings.context: Recap: greedy Clutch clipped his sheep bare, and one by one the whole flock vanished. With nothing left, Clutch and his gentle brother Kind climbed the hills, where music led them to a violet pasture, white sheep, and a very old shepherd. The story is still being told by Snowflower’s magic chair. A wallet here is a bag for food. Leathern means made of leather. Shaggy means with long, rough hair. Fleece is a sheep’s wool. Little-worth means not worth much.
readings.contentNote: A pack of howling wolves shows its teeth, and Clutch fears they will eat the brothers. No one is hurt.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Greedy Shepherd,” from Kind greeting the ancient shepherd to the end of the chair’s story; opens “"'Good father,' said Kind, for his eldest brother hung back and was afraid, 'tell us what…”; closes “…till this day, but Clutch has grown less greedy, and Kind alone uses the shears."”.

questions.prompt: How does Clutch describe himself when the old man asks who can shear best?
facilitatorNotes: As the closest shearer in all the plain, who leaves not enough wool for a thread; the boast he is proud of.
evidence: I am the closest shearer in all the plain country

questions.prompt: Who is the flock Clutch must shear? What does he do?
facilitatorNotes: A troop of shaggy wolves. He throws down the shears and hides behind the old man.
evidence: Clutch was glad to throw down his shears, and run behind the old man for safety

questions.prompt: How does Kind shear the wolves? Why do they stand still for him?
facilitatorNotes: Neatly but not too close, the way he wanted the sheep sheared. They seem to know him; they turn out to be his own lost sheep.
evidence: Kind clipped neatly, but not too close
the wild creature seemed to know him

questions.prompt: At the end, Clutch has “grown less greedy, and Kind alone uses the shears.” Is this a happy ending for Clutch too?
facilitatorNotes: Yes and no: he loses the flock to his brother and becomes the helper, but he gets home, is welcomed, and grows less greedy. Some children will say he got off lightly; others that losing his pride was enough.
evidence: Clutch has grown less greedy, and Kind alone uses the shears
